submission.natural_language_explanation: N380 is a formal-schooling unit: its pre-activation is a signed 'is this context about school and study' score, so the negative pole is exactly zero on schooling vocabulary and through clauses that are about schooling (school, university, college, campus, student, teacher, professor, faculty, lecture, exam, degree, tuition, classes, dropped out of school), and it goes negative everywhere else. The negative pole therefore fires once the text is off the schooling topic and grows with the distance from it - at or near zero (<=0.08) in schooling clauses and abstract academic prose, 0.04-0.28 in short everyday sentences, ~0.1-0.44 in encyclopedic/technical prose, 0.27-0.50 in narrative fiction, literary, markup or code text, and up to 0.80 on a single non-school word that breaks a schooling clause ('hospital' in 'She attended classes every morning at the hospital' reaches the pole's maximum, while 'university' in the same slot scores 0.00).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The lighthouse keeper trimmed the wick at dusk and logged the wind in a salt-stained ledger. Gulls hammered the lantern glass as the tide dragged kelp across the rocks below. He brewed coffee on the iron stove, mended a torn oilskin with waxed thread, and tuned the shortwave radio until a freighter captain answered through static. By midnight the foghorn moaned every ninety seconds, shaking dust from the rafters. He polished the Fresnel lens with vinegar and newspaper, counted the gull nests on the north ledge, and reset the brass barometer that always read low before a gale. Rain found the cracked shutter hinge again, so he wedged it with cork and lashed the spare rope coil against the gallery rail. Dawn arrived grey and dripping, the sea heaving white around the reef markers. He rowed ashore for kerosene, salt pork, nails, and lamp oil, trading mackerel with the harbor chandler for a discount on rope. Back on the rock he scraped barnacles from the landing steps, repainted the red band on the tower, and replaced a warped tread on the spiral stair. The afternoon brought a squall that tore the flag halyard loose; he spliced it with cold fingers while the wind tried to take his cap. He fed the keeper cat scraps of smoked haddock, swept sand from the watch room, and oiled the winch that hauled fuel drums up the cliff track. At sunset a yacht signaled for the channel bearing, and he flashed the lamp twice in reply before the automatic rotator took over. He ate beans from a tin, read a tide table by lamplight, and noted the moonrise over the breakwater. The night watch passed with fog signals, passing trawlers, and the slow sweep of the beam across black water. Near three in the morning the auxiliary pump rattled, and he bled air from the line with a wrench kept warm in his pocket. He checked the cistern level, patched a gutter seam with tar, and hung his wet socks near the stove pipe. When the sky paled he extinguished the lamp, covered the lens against the sun, and walked the cliff path to gather driftwood for the evening fire.
